checks.claim: Key: the Atlantic season peaks in early September because the sea goes on warming all summer
checks.note: NOAA: statistical peak 10 September; warming tropical ocean temperatures build with summer sun, plus wind shear at a minimum by mid to late August and African waves. The sea's slow warming is the right single answer at this level.

checks.claim: Stem: the longest day comes in June; the peak is in early September, nearly three months later
checks.note: NESDIS: 'early September marks the peak'; 21 June to 10 September is about 2.7 months.

checks.claim: Context: hurricanes form only over sea water of about 26 C or warmer
checks.note: Grokipedia: at least 26.5 C; Wikipedia: commonly accepted minimum 26-27 C; NESDIS about 80 F. 'About 26 degrees' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Context: the tropical Atlantic is near its warmest in late September; calmer winds aloft help set the peak on about 10 September
checks.note: DeMaria (NOAA): on sea temperature alone the peak would come in late September or early October, when tropical Atlantic SSTs are near their annual peak; NOAA story gives shear's minimum in mid to late August.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth passes closest to the Sun in September
checks.note: Perihelion falls about 2-5 January. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the Sun gives off the most heat in September
checks.note: The Sun's output varies by about a tenth of a percent or less over its 11-year cycle and not with Earth's seasons; the sunlight reaching Earth peaks at perihelion in early January. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the trade winds stop blowing by September; context: they blow all year and steer young storms west
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'persistent easterly surface winds', seasonal variation in strength only; they 'serve as primary steering currents, directing developing storms westward'. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: meteorologists call a hurricane a heat engine turning heat into the motion of its winds
checks.note: Grokipedia: heat engines 'converting thermal energy extracted from the ocean surface into mechanical energy', mainly via latent heat of condensation.

checks.claim: Key: water vapour condensing into droplets releases the heat high in the clouds
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Upon condensation within clouds, this latent heat is released, warming the surrounding air'; 'the subsequent condensation in eyewall clouds releases heat that fuels updrafts'. NASA: condensing vapour 'releases energy, or latent heat'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: evaporation and melting release the heat
checks.note: Evaporation absorbs latent heat (it cools the surface); melting absorbs heat. Both truly wrong. (Freezing, which does release heat, is not offered.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: sunlight warming the cloud tops
checks.note: The storm's energy is latent heat released in rising air, not sunlight on its clouds. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the released heat warms the air so it rises faster and draws in more moist air from the sea
checks.note: NASA: the heat boosts buoyancy, surface pressure falls, a feedback chain reaction draws in more air.

checks.claim: Stem: hurricanes almost never form within about 5 degrees of latitude of the equator
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'cyclones rarely form within 5 degrees of the equator'; Grokipedia: formation 'at least 5 degrees latitude poleward of the equator'. NASA gives 'generally at least 8 degrees', so 'about 5' and 'almost never' are safe.

checks.claim: Key: Earth's spin barely twists the air there (Coriolis zero at the equator, growing poleward)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'At the equator, f = 0; at the poles, f = 2 Omega'; Tropical cyclone page: equatorial regions lack sufficient rotational force.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: the equatorial air sinks / is too dry / blows too hard
checks.note: ITCZ: converging trades force air upward, moisture-laden, persistent thunderstorms, minimal winds in its core (the doldrums). None of the three is the textbook reason; all truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: only a very few storms, such as Typhoon Vamei in 2001, have formed closer in
checks.note: Vamei formed about 1.4-1.5 N in the South China Sea on 26 December 2001, a record for formation latitude (Cyclone Agni 2004 later came within 0.7 N). Wikipedia now titles it 'Tropical Storm Vamei' (JMA rated it a tropical storm; JTWC a typhoon, 75 mph, with an eye), so 'Typhoon Vamei' is defensible. Optional: 'the storm Vamei'.

checks.claim: Stem: every hurricane north of the equator turns counter-clockwise
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern'; tropical cyclones are always cyclonic.

checks.claim: Key: clockwise, as Earth's spin bends air the other way
checks.note: Deflection 'to the right of the motion in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere'; air flowing in toward the low is turned accordingly.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: clockwise because the seasons run the other way; counter-clockwise because Earth spins one way; either way by chance
checks.note: The seasons come from axial tilt and do not set the spin; the southern storms turn clockwise, not counter-clockwise; their turn is set by Coriolis, not chance. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a draining sink is too small for Earth's spin to steer, so it can swirl either way
checks.note: Grokipedia calls the hemisphere-drain belief 'a myth'; swirl set by basin shape and residual spin.

checks.claim: Stem: Hurricane John formed in the Pacific off Mexico in August 1994 and lasted about a month
checks.note: Formed 11 August 1994 south-southeast of Acapulco; lasted about 31 days (11 August to 10 September). No record is claimed, so Cyclone Freddy's 36 days (2023) does not touch the question.

checks.claim: Stem: partway through, forecasters began calling it Typhoon John
checks.note: Crossed the International Date Line about 27-28 August and was renamed Typhoon John by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

checks.claim: Key: the new name marked that it had moved into another part of the ocean
checks.note: NOAA: 'The only difference between a hurricane and a typhoon is the location where the storm occurs'; hurricane in the North Atlantic, central and eastern North Pacific; typhoon in the Northwest Pacific.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: faster winds, larger size, reversed spin
checks.note: The name is regional only; John stayed in the Northern Hemisphere and kept turning counter-clockwise. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: renamed at the Date Line, where the western Pacific begins; back east in September it was Hurricane John again
checks.note: It crossed back east on 8 September (by then a tropical storm) and regained hurricane strength on 9 September, so it was Hurricane John again. A fair compression.

checks.claim: Stem: Joseph Duckworth, an Army pilot, flew a small two-seat trainer into a hurricane on the Texas coast in 1943
checks.note: Lt. Col. Joseph B. Duckworth, US Army Air Forces, 27 July 1943, AT-6 Texan single-engine trainer from Bryan Field, storm crossing the upper Texas coast (landfall Bolivar Peninsula). The AT-6 is a tandem two-seat trainer (watchers.news: 'two-seat AT-6 Texan trainer'; Smithsonian NASM).

checks.claim: Stem: the first known flight made on purpose into a hurricane's eye
checks.note: The Monthly Weather Review (Nov 1943) called it 'the first time, to our knowledge, that a plane has been intentionally flown through the center of a hurricane', and Grokipedia says the first documented intentional penetration of an eye. But NWS Houston's account, from O'Hair, says the flight was a bet to fly into the storm and that reaching the eye 'was not the purpose of the flight, but really an accident'. All sources agree it was the first known flight made on purpose into a hurricane. Fix: 'the first known flight made on purpose into a hurricane.'

checks.claim: Stem: violent bumps and pounding rain, then calm air with the Sun above and the ground in view below
checks.note: 1943 report: in the eye they 'could see the sun and the ground'; Grokipedia: intense turbulence, heavy rain, near-darkness, then calm with a clear view of the countryside; O'Hair: 'tossed about like a stick in a dog's mouth'.

checks.claim: Key: the eye's air sinks, and sinking air makes no clouds
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'descending air subsidence, which warms and dries the atmosphere, suppressing cloud formation'; NASA: 'a cloud-free area of sinking air and light winds'; Wikipedia: at the centre 'air sinks rather than rises'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: air rising too fast for clouds; winds from every side meeting and cancelling; cold air pooling
checks.note: Rising air makes clouds, not clears them; inflowing air turns up in the eyewall and never reaches the centre (rotation balances the pressure pull), so nothing meets and cancels; the eye is a warm core, 5-10 C warmer than its surroundings. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: light breezes, lowest pressure, warm core several degrees warmer, eyewall a ring of towering thunderstorms
checks.note: Eye winds typically under 15 mph; pressure minimum at the centre; 'warmer than the surrounding environment by 5-10 C'; eyewall 'a ring of towering thunderstorms with the storm's strongest winds'.

checks.claim: Context: on a second flight that day the weather officer William Jones-Burdick recorded temperatures inside it (the eye)
checks.note: Dorst (Weatherwise 2024, NOAA repository) credits Jones-Burdick with the first temperature readings taken while flying into a hurricane; Grokipedia instead says he recorded winds and pressure; the 1943 report and NWS Houston name him only. Temperatures in the storm are supported; temperatures inside the eye specifically, tied to the warm core, are not. Fix: '...recorded temperatures inside the storm.'

checks.claim: Key: after the calm eye passes, fierce winds return from the opposite direction
checks.note: NPS: 'Then the eyewall approaches from the opposite direction, and the chaos starts all over again.' Grokipedia (Eye): 'the most intense winds return shortly after the eye passes'. A station on the track sees the wind reverse because the winds circle the centre.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: fierce winds from the same way; light winds as the storm has blown out; light rain from outer bands
checks.note: The far eyewall comes next, not the rain bands or the end of the storm, and its winds blow from the reverse side of the circulation. All truly wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: calm and blue sky within minutes as the eye arrives
checks.note: NPS: 'It's sunny, the winds are calm, and birds are in the air.' Eye winds typically under 15 mph (Grokipedia).

checks.claim: Context: the eyewall has the strongest winds; sailors took the calm for the storm's end; forecasters warn the worst winds return
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'early sailors frequently misinterpreted the eye's calm as the storm's conclusion'. 'As fierce as before' is a fair simplification (the back side can be somewhat weaker or stronger depending on the storm's motion); optional: 'fierce again'.

checks.claim: Stem: Herbert Saffir, an engineer, and Robert Simpson, a meteorologist, made the scale in the early 1970s; five categories
checks.note: NPS: 'In the early 1970s, Herbert Saffir, an engineer, and Robert Simpson, a meteorologist, developed a scale'; Grokipedia: developed 1971, Simpson then NHC director; Categories 1-5.

checks.claim: Stem and context: since 2010 the scale rates by strongest sustained winds alone and leaves out storm surge
checks.note: Surge and pressure ranges were removed in 2009-2010; renamed the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale in 2010; rated by maximum 1-minute sustained winds.

checks.claim: Key: storm surge is the danger often the deadliest
checks.note: NOAA: 'The greatest threat to life actually comes from the water - in the form of storm surge.' Rappaport (NHC, 2014) for US deaths 1963-2012: surge 49%. Newer figures put freshwater flooding first in the US (2013-2022: 57% flood, 11% surge; 1963-2024: 36% vs 33%), so 'often' is the right word and the question survives.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: strongest winds, tornadoes, lightning
checks.note: The scale is built on the winds, so they are not left out; tornadoes (3%) and lightning are left out but are not often the deadliest. Only surge fits the stem.

checks.claim: Context: surge about half the deaths 1963-2012, wind 8 percent, tornadoes 3; surge pushed ashore by the winds
checks.note: Rappaport 2014: surge 49%, rain floods 27%, surf 6%, offshore 6%, wind 8%, tornadoes 3%. NOAA: surge 'caused primarily by a storm's winds pushing water onshore'.

checks.claim: Context: Ike was a Category 2 as it neared Texas in 2008, with a surge typical of a Category 4 or 5
checks.note: NPS: 'Ike downgraded to a category 2 hurricane as it approached the Texas shoreline' and 'caused storm surge typical of a category 4 or 5 hurricane'.

checks.claim: Stem: dropsondes are instrument packs that fall by parachute and radio back the wind
checks.note: Grokipedia: deployed from aircraft, descends under a parachute, measures pressure, temperature, humidity and wind (GPS), transmitting in real time; used on NOAA hurricane reconnaissance.

checks.claim: Stem: a hurricane over 20 C water weakens day by day; another weakens just as fast ashore
checks.note: Dissipation over waters 'significantly cooler than 26.5 C' and over land is standard. A scenario, not a rule; land decay is often faster than over cool sea, so optional wording: 'Another hurricane weakens too after it moves ashore.'

checks.claim: Key: each has lost its supply of warm, moist air
checks.note: NASA: cooler water 'can't supply warm, moist tropical air'; land is 'again cutting off the source of warm, moist air'. NOAA Ocean Explorer agrees.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: each has moved where Earth's spin is weaker
checks.note: f grows from 0 at the equator to 2 Omega at the poles; moving north makes it stronger, moving ashore does not change it. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: cold air freezes its clouds; context: the high cloud tops are frozen already, at about -70 C
checks.note: Grokipedia: outflow temperature at the tropopause 'typically around -70 C (200 K)'; NASA infrared readings of hurricane tops run from about -55 C to -80 C (often quoted as -70 F), well below freezing, so the tops are ice. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: too little sunlight; context: the heat comes from the sea
checks.note: The engine is latent heat from sea-warmed vapour; storms run day and night. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: over land, rough ground slows the winds as well
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'surface friction from continental terrain significantly increases drag on the near-surface winds'.

unit_notes: Sources were read 2026-11-26. One question uncertain (3eb230897e, the Duckworth flight): two small wording fixes, no physics at issue. Things that change over time: (1) US hurricane death shares now put freshwater flooding ahead of surge (NHC 2013-2022: 57% vs 11%; npj study 1963-2024: 36% vs 33%); the surge question says 'often' and dates its 1963-2012 figure, so it survives. (2) John's 31 days was passed by Cyclone Freddy (36 days, 2023); the question claims no record. (3) Vamei is now titled 'Tropical Storm Vamei' on Wikipedia (JMA tropical storm, JTWC typhoon); 'Typhoon Vamei' is defensible. Latitude limit: Grokipedia and Wikipedia give 5 degrees, NASA about 8; 'within about 5 degrees' with 'almost never' is safe.
